title: Ask Before the Write: When an MCP Tool Should Elicit
excerpt: A missing target gets invented. Elicitation is how an MCP server pauses a tool call and asks the person — and the 2026-07-28 spec is what makes that pause work without a session.
coverImageAlt: Three cards: a confirmation form before a delete, a URL that keeps a secret off the client, and a second tool call that carries the answer
newsletterIntro: A tool that is missing a target will invent one. Elicitation is the pause: the server stops the call and asks the person before it deletes, spends, or collects a secret. Spec 2026-07-28 is what makes that pause work on a stateless server.
newsletterPullQuote: Confirm the cost. Confirm the delete. Leave the model out of the blank it was about to fill.
contentHtml:
A model that is missing a target will invent one. A prompt that says “ask before you delete” is a suggestion. The tool still runs.

Elicitation is the pause. The server stops the call and asks the person, through the client, before it spends money, deletes rows, or sends the person somewhere else to type a secret. Spec revision 2026-07-28 is what makes that pause work on the servers people actually host: stateless HTTPS, any instance, no held-open stream.

On the specification announcement, Inian Parameshwaran, head of product at Supabase, wrote that elicitations had been on their roadmap and that a stateless server made the old flow impractical. Multi-round-trip requests change that. Their tools can confirm with the user before acting: the cost of a new project before it is created, or a query that would delete data. Brendan Irvine-Broque, writing for Cloudflare in the same post, described the same capability as richer flows like elicitation for approvals.

That is the piece worth shipping. Confirm the cost. Confirm the delete. Leave the model out of the blank it was about to fill.

A sentence in the prompt is not the ask

The argument developers are already having splits MCP into two piles. A server that duplicates a CLI the model knows is a tax. A server that holds a credential the agent cannot read is a boundary. On the September 20, 2026 Hacker News thread, simonw’s case for keeping a server was the tighter setup: control over which services the agent can reach, authentication that does not hand the agent the key, and an audit log of what was called. A line in the prompt does not do that job.

Elicitation is the boundary for a different moment. The tool is allowed to exist. It is not allowed to finish until a person answers a question the tool could not know up front. “The model will ask” is the sentence. elicitation/create is the question, rendered by the client, with decline and cancel as real outcomes.

Before July 28, 2026 that question was a server-initiated request on a stream the server had to keep open. Hosts that scale like any other HTTPS API could not keep it. The multi-round-trip pattern replaces it. The spec calls this a breaking change: servers must send elicitation/create as an input_required result. The same pattern is how sampling and roots requests travel while those features still exist. The previous server-initiated pattern is no longer supported.

Two ways to ask

The elicitation spec has two modes. They are not interchangeable.

Form mode sends a human-readable message and a requestedSchema. The client renders a form. The answer comes back on the retry, in content, and the client can see it. The schema is small on purpose: a flat object whose fields are strings, numbers, booleans, or enums. Nested objects are out. A boolean named confirm fits. An enum of the three projects the tool just found fits. A multi-step wizard does not.

URL mode sends a message and a URL. The person finishes the interaction on that URL, outside the client. An accept means they consented to open the link. It does not mean the interaction finished. The spec says the client is not told the outcome. On the retry, the server looks at the echoed requestState, or at state it stored itself, and either completes the call or returns input_required again.

Secrets have a hard rule. Servers must not use form mode to request passwords, API keys, access tokens, or payment credentials. Those interactions must use URL mode, so the secret never passes through the MCP client or the model’s context. A name, an email, or a username is not in that forbidden list. A credential is.

URL mode is also not how a client logs into your MCP server. The spec says servers must not rely on URL elicitation to authorize users for themselves. That job is MCP authorization. Third-party credentials obtained through URL mode must not transit the client, and the server must not send them back to the client. The URL itself must not carry the secret, personal data, or a pre-authenticated link a malicious client could open as the user.

One capability detail bites people who only test the happy client. An empty elicitation object means form only. The spec says so, for backwards compatibility. Servers must not send a mode the client did not declare. A confirm-delete form works against an empty capability. A browser login does not. Read the capability object on the request. A README that says “supports elicitation” is not that object.

The pause is a second HTTP call

The round trip is ordinary request/response. There is no session to resume.

  1. The client sends tools/call.
  2. The server decides it needs a person and returns resultType: "input_required", an inputRequests map, and an optional requestState string. That HTTP call is finished.
  3. The client shows the question and collects an answer, or the person declines, or they dismiss it.
  4. The client retries tools/call with a new JSON-RPC id, the original arguments, an inputResponses map keyed the same way, and the requestState echoed exactly.
  5. The server completes the tool, or it asks again.

input_required is legal on tools/call, prompts/get, and resources/read. It is not a result you can hang on every method.

A confirm looks like this on the wire. The ids and the state blob are the server’s; the shape is the spec’s.

{
  "jsonrpc": "2.0",
  "id": 1,
  "result": {
    "resultType": "input_required",
    "inputRequests": {
      "confirm_delete": {
        "method": "elicitation/create",
        "params": {
          "mode": "form",
          "message": "Delete 1,204 rows in production?",
          "requestedSchema": {
            "type": "object",
            "properties": {
              "confirm": { "type": "boolean", "title": "Delete the rows" }
            },
            "required": ["confirm"]
          }
        }
      }
    },
    "requestState": "<opaque, integrity-protected>"
  }
}

The retry carries the answer under the same key:

{
  "confirm_delete": {
    "action": "accept",
    "content": { "confirm": true }
  }
}

requestState is opaque to the client. Clients must not inspect, parse, or modify it. Because it travels through the client, the server treats it as attacker-controlled. If it influences which row is deleted or who is allowed to delete it, the spec requires integrity protection — it names HMAC or AEAD — and rejection when the check fails. It also says servers should bind that protected state to the authenticated principal, give it a short expiry, and tie it to the originating call so it cannot be replayed onto a different tool. That bounds replay. It does not make the action exactly once. If a given state must be consumed a single time, the server enforces that itself.

Sampling and roots can ride in the same inputRequests map. Both are deprecated as of 2026-07-28. They keep working for at least twelve months. New implementations should not adopt them. The request you want in that map is elicitation/create. The rest of what to rip out of that revision is the deprecation-clock checklist.

Ask for a decision the schema could not know

Elicitation is a poor patch for a tool whose input schema is incomplete.

If every successful call needs a project id, put the project id on the tool. The client can require it before the handler runs. A mid-call form that collects a parameter you forgot to declare teaches the model to fire a half-specified tool and wait. The user-interaction section of the spec leaves the UI to the client. It does not invite servers to interview the user for fields that belonged in tools/list.

Elicit when the answer depends on something the tool just learned, or when a person has to approve a consequence:

  • The lookup returned three customers and only one of them is the target.
  • The SQL is valid, and it deletes rows. That is Supabase’s example, not a metaphor.
  • Creating the project has a price, and the price was not in the prompt.

Fail the call, with a clear error, when the client did not declare the mode you need, or when you would otherwise proceed on a default the user never saw. A default of “yes” on a delete is the bug elicitation exists to remove.

Accept, decline, and the dialog that just closed

The spec’s response has three actions, and they are not synonyms.

  • Accept is an explicit submit. On a form, content matches the schema. On a URL, content is omitted: the person agreed to open the link, and the out-of-band step may still be unfinished.
  • Decline is an explicit no. The person chose not to provide it.
  • Cancel is a dismissal without a choice: the dialog closed, Escape, the page never loaded.

Servers must handle decline, cancel, and a client that fails to complete the request. The spec also says they should not assume an elicitation succeeds. A handler that treats a missing retry as accept will delete rows because a laptop lid closed. Decline can offer another path. Cancel should stop. Neither is permission to guess.

Do the write on the second call

The first request ends when you return input_required. The retry is a different request, with a different JSON-RPC id, and on a stateless deployment it can land on a different instance. That is why the context lives in requestState instead of in a session.

The irreversible work belongs on the retry, after accept, after the state checks out. Inserting the row or starting the charge before you ask turns decline and cancel into a cleanup problem, and a replayed retry can do the work twice. The protocol does not offer exactly-once. If you already mutated something, you own the rollback.

A hook can remove the person

Claude Code’s hooks reference, read on November 11, 2026, documents an Elicitation hook. The default is a dialog. A hook can answer for the user: return action: "accept" and the form fields, and the dialog never appears. On a URL-mode request, the same accept skips the dialog, so the URL never opens. Decline and cancel are available the same way, including by exiting with code 2.

The hook is a reasonable policy gate. Refuse URL elicitations from servers you have not named. Log the question. It is a bad place to auto-confirm a delete. An elicitation a script answers is a prompt with extra steps. The person was the control. I am not claiming every host has this hook. I am claiming the spec’s safety story assumes someone can decline, and a host that answers for them has turned that into a policy you chose.

What a handshake cannot tell you

A handshake proves the endpoint spoke MCP and returned tools/list. It does not prove a write tool asks first. On a server page, the clue is the verb: delete, drop, charge, send, create-with-a-cost. The confirmation behavior is inside the handler. You see it by reading the source or by calling the tool in a sandbox. Until that story exists, ship eyes before hands.

A form that asks for an API key is a spec violation, not a login flow. Paste-a-key is still dead, and secrets still do not belong in MCP headers or in form fields. If the server needs a third-party account, that is URL mode, on a client that declared url, with the secret staying on the other site.

If you are building the server, the practical bar is short:

  1. Elicit a decision the input schema could not know. Put everything else on the tool.
  2. Return input_required before any side effect.
  3. Use a form for a confirm or a pick. Use a URL for a secret or a third-party authorization. Never a form for a credential.
  4. Handle accept, decline, cancel, and a client that never comes back.
  5. Integrity-protect requestState, bind it to the user and the call, and make one-time actions one-time on the server.

Then put the server where someone can handshake it. The directory can show the tool names. It cannot show the pause. The pause is yours to implement.

Quick answers

Does input_required mean the tool succeeded?

No. It means the server stopped and asked. The tool result is a later response, after the client retries.

Is a URL-mode accept proof the user finished signing in?

No. It is consent to open the URL. The server checks requestState or its own store on the retry, and it may return input_required again.

Can a form collect a password if the field is labeled secret?

No. The 2026-07-28 elicitation spec forbids form mode for passwords, API keys, access tokens, and payment credentials. Those go through URL mode.

Does an empty elicitation capability include URL mode?

No. The spec treats an empty elicitation object as form only. Servers must not send a mode the client did not declare.

Should a new server adopt sampling in the same round trip?

No. Sampling is deprecated as of 2026-07-28, with at least twelve months before removal. Use elicitation when a person has to decide.
